description: We’re a team of two, a UI/UX designer and a programmer - with a shared passion for space and tackling new challenges. We love combining design and technology to turn complex ideas into intuitive, useful experiences.
summary:
Trend Detective is a web app that helps anyone check whether a climate variable has changed at a place on Earth, and how sure we can be.

Users pick a location on a 3D globe or on 2D maps of countries, reaching down to municipalities in Austria and counties in the USA. The app then pulls live data from NASA POWER: monthly temperature, precipitation, relative humidity and wind, plus daily data for extremes.

For any time span the user chooses, it estimates a linear trend per decade using ordinary least squares with HAC standard errors, which account for year-to-year autocorrelation. It reports the trend with its p-value and 95% confidence interval, and says in plain language whether the trend is statistically clear, meaning the interval excludes zero.

Results export as CSV, JSON or Excel, with the data source and spatial method included.

This addresses the challenge by turning Earth observation data into trend statements people can check for themselves. It matters because claims about a changing climate are everywhere, and Trend Detective shows both the change and its uncertainty instead of a single number.

The source code is open on GitHub: [https://github.com/mancinisamuel/nasa-trend-detective-project](https://github.com/mancinisamuel/nasa-trend-detective-project)

The presentation is also available here in case the production server does not work: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1j8fRy-v84FFCK8_-9D4sKgZbvAZaVz77/view?usp=sharing
details:
Trend Detective is an interactive web app for exploring climate trends in Austria and the United States. Users pick a place on a 3D globe or search for it, choose a time range, and explore changes in temperature, rainfall, hot days, and more. They can view annual values, check trends, and export the data to Excel. We designed it as a detective-style investigation so students and the public can start with a familiar place and follow their own questions.

How the numbers are calculated

All climate values come from NASA POWER’s roughly 50 km grid. Towns use the cell they sit in. States average the cells that overlap them, giving more weight to cells with more area inside the state. National averages weight states by area.

The app fits a trend to the annual values and reports the change per decade, a confidence interval, and a significance test that accounts for similarities between consecutive years. Indicators like hot days and tropical nights use daily data from the town’s cell or, for a state, its capital’s cell. The app explains which method it used and warns when the selected period is short.

Tools, languages and software

We built the app with Python 3.12, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, and three.js, and used geoBoundaries for administrative boundaries. We use pytest and Vitest for around 400 tests and cache data to reduce requests to NASA POWER. The app runs in a standard web browser with no special hardware. AI assistants helped with code and text. The calculations use no AI.
